The famous ship that sank in 1912 after hitting an iceberg is the RMS Titanic.

To understand blockchain technology, imagine a massive, shared notebook that is kept by thousands of people all over the world. In a traditional system, like a bank, only one person (the bank) holds the official notebook and writes down who has how much money. If that person makes a mistake or tries to cheat, it’s hard to prove otherwise because you don’t have a copy of the book.

In a blockchain system, everyone has their own copy of this notebook. Every time a new transaction happens, it’s like writing a new page in the notebook. Before that page is added, everyone checks to make sure the math adds up and that the person writing it actually has the money they claim to have. Once the majority agrees the page is correct, it is added to everyone’s notebook at the same time.

Because everyone has a copy, no single person can change a past entry without everyone else noticing. If someone tried to sneak in and erase a line in their own notebook, the other thousands of notebooks would still show the original entry, and the change would be rejected. This makes the record extremely secure and trustworthy, as it relies on the collective agreement of the group rather than a single central authority.
